title: Fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing with a single nucleus per node
authors: Yotam Vaknin, Shoham Jaocby, Roi Nevo, Aleksander Kubica, Alex Retzker
abstract: Distributed quantum computing interconnects small, high-quality nodes through optical links, but this architecture carries a pronounced asymmetry: in-node gates and measurements are cheap and high-fidelity, whereas inter-node communication relies on a low-coherence communication qubit and faulty photonics. Previous approaches overcame the noisy link by placing several high-quality data qubits in each node and consuming them for Bell pair and GHZ state distillation. Here we show that distillation can be avoided altogether. The key observation is that we can engineer a communication error bias, where photonic Bell pairs suffer frequent phase errors but only rare bit-flip errors. We design the syndrome-extraction circuits so that this phase noise appears solely as a measurement error that does not propagate to the data qubits, and is therefore suppressed by simply repeating the measurement; letting the error-correcting code itself, rather than a dedicated distillation subroutine, to purify the link. This dramatically reduces the need for ancillary nuclei: Floquet codes require only a single data qubit per node, while general stabilizer codes require just one additional ancilla. We demonstrate high error-correction thresholds throughout this regime, and we identify lattice surgery as inherently robust for this setting, enabling logical operations at a threshold close to that of quantum memory. As a result, the performance of the quantum computer is limited by the high-quality data qubits, while the requirements on photon indistinguishability and coherence of the communication qubit are substantially relaxed.
summary: The paper presents a novel approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing that bypasses resource-intensive state distillation. By exploiting an engineered error bias in photonic links—where phase errors are common but bit-flips are rare—the required ancillary qubits per node are drastically reduced. This makes the performance limited by the high-quality local memory rather than the noisy communication channel.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving fault-tolerant distributed quantum computation while minimizing the required number of ancillary qubits per node.
main_result: By engineering a communication error bias (phase errors dominant), the need for dedicated state distillation can be avoided, significantly reducing resource overhead and relaxing link fidelity requirements.
method: The authors design syndrome-extraction circuits that exploit this phase noise bias, allowing simple measurement repetition to suppress errors using the error-correcting code itself rather than complex purification protocols.
model_or_system: The system models distributed quantum nodes interconnected via optical links. Each node utilizes high-fidelity nuclear spins for data qubits and low-coherence electron spins for communication qubits.
key_observables: Logical error rate, error correction thresholds (e.g., Honeycomb code threshold up to pz ~ 11%), and the required number of ancillary qubits per node.
important_parameters: Phase error probability ($p_z$), residual noise strength ($p_{	ext{res}}$), and the ratio between these two error types, which defines the exploitable bias.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the dominant noise contribution is phase noise affecting generated Bell pairs, allowing it to be treated as a measurement error rather than propagating directly to data qubits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate implementing Floquet QEC protocols using minimal ancillary qubits and show how repeating measurements significantly raises the threshold for phase errors in both Honeycomb and Hyperbolic codes compared to single measurements.
paper_structure: The paper develops theory by first identifying the resource bottleneck (distillation) and proposing a solution based on error bias. It then analyzes performance thresholds using specific codes (Floquet/stabilizer) and discusses stability improvements through measurement repetition, concluding with detailed circuit implementations for state preparation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides concrete, resource-efficient protocols for scaling quantum computation across physically separated modules, directly impacting the feasibility of large-scale quantum networks.
